chapter: Style and solos in the early bands
title: Celestin playing endless choruses at the Temple
summary: He tells of Celestin soloing chorus after chorus while others took down, and that orchestrations were played short.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Who would take down? Yeah. Well, if the trumpet player might want to take a solo. Oh, after three ensembles he'd still be strong enough? Man, Celestine looked like he played for hours. Man, Celestine was playing up on the bandstand with us at the temple, I swear to God. He played a tune so long it was pitiful. I'm telling you, it was not nastush, you know. Ain't nothing but chorus. It's the same thing, you know. Man, that man would play chorus, man, after chorus, chorus after chorus. Wouldn't allow us to play nothing. Man, he went over there and asked him, say, what you doing, man, playing about a hour or what? That answer he played so long, I thought, oh, man. He'd take down and the trombone and all the rest of them would play. All right, he'd put up. Then the trombone, I guess he's tired, that's why he'd take now, you know. And the clarinet, then he'd put up, the trombone put up. Then him and Celestine would play. Then the clarinet would take down. Nothing but the rhythm, jump, jump, jump, jump, jump, jump, jump.
Then they'd pick up a, oh, man, I swear to God, that people played so long, man. Oh, man.

Now, the only time they would play short, they'd play orchestration, you see. Well, they'd play it down. And if it was a good orchestration, you know, that they liked, well, they'd go back to the chorus and play one or two, you see. Of course, Celestine always read music, just like Manuel Perez, you see. Always had musicians in their reach, you know. It felt like Buddy Pettine, you know.
